the profound respect to your honorable body to ad-
comport with your duty and inclination TO grant, in
utterance of the objects hereinafter set forth Your
petitioner would in the first place state to your hon-
orable body that the present condition Of the Sixteenth
ward such as in the opinion Of your petitioner and
of other residents in said ward will inevitably produce
some deadly epidemic If measures for removing the
filth now rotting and reeking in many of the streets
thereof, be not speedily adopted. Anxious that the
ward should escape the threatened visitation your peti-
tioner respectfully solicits from your honorable body
permission to supervise without compensation the
cleansing of the public streets Of said ward, will
cheerfully give bonus for the faithful application
of funds necessary For that purpose and receipts AND vouch
for every item of expenditure, If your honorable
body should allow, which amount, your Petitioner believes would not
exceed $50 per week. Your petitioner addresses your
honorable body, which committee OF the Board Of Councilmen has recently bestowed
upon the course Of action pursued by that department.
In conclusion your petitioner would respectfully state
that if he has failed in wording this his petition in
suitable to the dignity of your august established
and honorable body, his shortcomings should be attribu-
ted to his ignorance OF the forms and
provided not to his lack Of humility or Of that
and gratitude which, citizen OF New York he
owes the honorable body for the protection it vouchsafes to
his life, health and property. Hoping that this his
petition may find favor in the sight OF your honorable
body your petitioner in duty bound will ever pray
&c JOHN N. GENIN.


Mr. JOHNSON said as one of the representa-
tives OF the Tenth ward, he would say that they had
no right to give out any further contracts. The
charter of 1858 forbid any such action on their
part.


MR. KENNEDY said that he desired to say a few
words relative to the petition. When the gentle-
man presented similar petition the other evening,
he asked for the reading Of it, so that the Board
might know the impudence OF the said Genin, and
was abused for it by all the newspapers who hold
Mr. Genin up for Mayor, and support his measure
for cleaning a ward at great deal higher price
than the gentlemen to whom the contract had al-
ready been awarded. MR. Genin offered to clean
the ward for $500 per week, while the contractor
offers to do it for $300. Now, in view Of those facts
he thought the offer Of Mr. Genin was not so very
patriotic after ALL. He then called Mr. Genin the
head scavenger of New York, and concluded by
saying that he would meet but little sympathy
among the members of the Common Council.


Mr. SEELY moved to lay the petition on the
table. Agreed.

That the sidewalks on Sixteenth avenue, between
123d and 129th street be cleaned under the direction
of the Street Commissioner. That the Commis-
sioner of Streets and Lamps be directed to transmit
to the Common Council Immediately, for confir-
mation the contracts for cleaning streets as reported
by him June, 1852.


CHANGE OF HOUR FOR MEETING.


On motion, the rules were changed by a two
third vote, so that the Board could meet every day
during the warm weather, except Saturdays and
Sundays, beginning at four o'clock, so that their
business could be finished in ten consecutive nights.
The motion to take effect on the 1st Of July.
REMOVING THE RAILS OF THE HARLEM RAILROAD
COMPANY FROM THE CITY.


BY Councilman MONAGHAN—Resolved that the
Street Commissioner be directed to take up the
rails of the Harlem Railroad Company in Centre
and Broome streets, Bowery and Fourth avenue to
Twenty street, and have the streets repaved
and placed in proper travelling order and that
$1,900 be appropriated therefor. Referred to Com-
mittee OF the Whole.


BY Councilman Curry—That Thirty-first street
be paved and repaired from Sixth to Eighth ave-
nues. Referred to Committee on Streets.


REPORTS OF COMMITTEES


A number Of unimportant reports were then read
and referred to the Committee of the Whole.

machine, and turning lathes. Block making
in all its branches is here carried on. Sabots
for shot and shell, wooden fuze stocks for
shrapnel, blue-light, and false fire cups, and
all other descriptions of turning are here ex-
ecuted. There are ten hands employed in this
department.

THE NEW FOUNDRY,

under the superintendent of Mr. Chief En-
gineer Hunt, Mr. William H. Bland, fore-
man. Here there is a steam engine (Mr.
combs Grinwell, engineer,) of about fifteen
horse power, blowing the fans for two cupola
furnaces, which are capable of melting metal
for the largest iron castings. There are, also,
large cylinder boring apparatus, screw
lathe for turning shafts, &c, and a planing
machine—all designed to execute the heaviest
iron work. In this building, shot, shells, bed
plates, and other castings are made. Here
the cylinder for the steamer Fulton, thirteen
feet in length, and fifty two inches inside
diameter, weighing 14,055 pounds, was re-
cently cast and finished. Over the machinery
in this building there is a depository for all
kinds of patterns for preservation. There are
thirty-seven hands employed in the iron foun-
dry at the present time. We will now pro-
ceed to take a view of

The BOILER SHOP,

under the direction of Mr. Chief Engineer
Hunt, (Mr. Thomas Champion, foreman.)
Here there is a small steam engine, (Mr. John
Serro, engineer,) of fifteen horse power with
a fan-blower attached, blowing thirty seven
furnaces in the boiler and smiths shops, and
driving the punching machine, shears, drills,
and grindstones in the boiler shop. In this
department there are low in course of manu-
facturing, buoys for the Light-
house Board of the Treasury Department, to
be distributed throughout the various bays,
rivers, and harbors of the country. Within
the past two years there have been manufac-
tures at this yard, and delivered to the light-
house board, one hundred buoys, complete,
of the first, second, and third classes. In this
department several steam boilers have been
manufactured for the engines built here, and
for various vessels; and the boilers for the
new steamer Minnesota (four in number)
are now in progress of construction. These
boilers are to be each eleven feet six inches
long, fourteen feet wide, and fourteen feet
deep, and will have a FIRE surface, each, of
5000 superficial feet. In the boiler shop
there are one hundred and one hands em-
ployed. Let us now pass into

THE SHIP SHAFTS AND CHAIN CABLE SHOP,

under the direction of Mr. James Tucker,
Messrs. William Morgan and Henry Oder,
all descriptions of iron forging for ship work
and machinery are done, and chain cables of
all sizes, from two and half inches diam-
eter to the smallest-size chain, are manufa-
ctured for the entire navy. The chains here
manufactured, long experience has demon-
strated, are equal, if not superior, to those
made in any part of the world—the iron for
chains being subjected to the severest tests
before it is received. In this building there
is also hydraulic proving machine for test-
ing each section (ninety feet of chain, after
having been manufactured. In connection
with this department there is likewise an iron
filing and finishing shop. There are ninety
hands employed in this establishment. Let
us next drop into

THE JOINER'S DEPARTMENT,

under the direction of Mr. H. B. Curran,
(Mr. Lewis Marceron, foreman.) Attached to
this building there is small steam-engine
for driving a circular saw, one of Wright's
upright scroll saws, one of Otis's machines,
and two tenonning machines. This is a spa-
cious and convenient shop for the execution
of all kinds of house-carpentry and ship-join-
ers work. The several beautiful and sub-
stantial buildings recently erected at the
yard, evidence the finished style and great
extent of the work done in this department.
There are fifty hands here employed. Annexed
to this joiner's shop is

THE YARD CARPENTERS, WHEELWRIGHTS, AND
COOPER'S SHOP,

under the direction of Mr. James K. McCath-
ran. The work here done, consists of fitting
frames for pile drivers, making timber heels,
carts, wheelbarrows, buckets, cans, &c., &c.
In this shop there are 10 hands employed.
The upper story of this building is occupied
by

THE MOULD LOFT AND NAVAL CONSTRUCTOR'S
OFFICE,

(Mr. H. Cook, naval constructor; Mr. Ed-
ward Foster, foreman.) This loft is 200 feet
in length, and 15 feet in width. There may
be seen models of large number of our na-
tional ships, some of which were built at this
yard, as also several designs for vessels here-
tofore proposed to be constructed. On this
floor the lines, preparatory to making the
moulds for the Minnesota, were laid down,
and may yet be seen. We will now pass on to

THE SHIP-HOUSE.

This structure was originally 232 feet in len-
gth, and about 10 feet in width. Lately, 72 feet
have been added to the eastern end, to give
length, under cover, for the building of the
Minnesota, making its present length 304.

WASHINGTON NEWS AND GOSSIP:


The Very Last Phase Of the present affairs --It seems from New York advices received yesterday morning that Captain Ticklepaust is mistaken in his understanding of the acts assumed by the commander of the British squadron now lying at Greytown. He has formally taken possession of that settlement, and has also assumed to hold Punta Arenas, being in dispute; the Mosquito King claiming it, being embraced within his pretended dominions in his proclamation; however, he expressly declares his intention to protect the business and property of the Transit Company, from molestation from any quarter whatever including any claim on the part of the Greytown people for indemnity for the act of Capt. Hollins. He gives the unprotected state of the people of Greytown as his reason for his act, their property remaining at the mercy of thieves and plunderers, and many of them being British subjects. He further expressly states, that his act of taking possession is not to be construed into an interference in the final settlement of the affair as an issue between the two Governments—the United States and Great Britain.

We doubted the fact of the taking possession yesterday, not only on account of the absence of dispatches from Mr. Fabens, which was currently believed among the diplomatists here but because We took it for granted that the British authorities in the West Indies are fully aware that Mr. Buchanan and Lord Clarendon have nearly completed a new treaty of Central American questions for the most part which has, for some time, been a subject of familiar conversation among foreign ministers and their aides resident here. We expected and continue to expect, that within the next thirty days treaty, as above referred to, will be concluded, in which Great Britain will very sensibly relinquish her ridiculous pretensions to territorial authority in that quarter.

However, We really rejoice that the commander of her West India squadron has taken a step which precludes any possibility that Britain may much longer delay a full and final settlement of the question of her right in that quarter, even though the expected treaty may not turn out as we hope. He has thus brought affairs there to a sudden and full issue, which is not to be shirked by either Government. Britain is hereafter to have, acknowledged, sovereign rights on the coast of Central America, or she is not to have them. We are hereafter to acknowledge them to be sovereign rights; or we are to disavow all such pretensions. A thorough knowledge of the history of her miserable attempts to fetch territory in that quarter, leads us to conclude that in the expected treaty she will renounce every point she has so far seemed to gain by them. In truth, she has no legal right to a square inch of soil on the coast of Central America under three treaties with Spain and Mexico. She has acquired the right to cut log wood at Belize, but acquire no territorial right whatever through them. The next step was the act of her royal map makers, who committed a deliberate fraud in calling Belize, British Honduras, when it was notorious to all the statesmen and geographers of both hemispheres, that it was no more British than Peruvian or Gillian, but a part of Yucatan—that is, of Mexico. Her next step was to claim that portion of the province of Vera Paz (an integral portion of the Republic of Guatemala) lying on the coast. Her third step was to steal the adjoining corner of the Republic of Honduras. This last-mentioned theft is the original and genuine Mosquito Protectorate.

Now comes the final act of meanness and mendacious theft which is, frankly, the commander of her West India squadron, to extend the authority of the miserable breathless savage of Blue Fields hundreds of miles so as to cover the mouth of the river San Juan Del Norte. This last attempt to steal territory in that quarter, is in positive violation of the Clayton and Bulwer treaty, and is, frankly, as crass of an act as if justified by the Home Government. People will remember that Nicholas,
when at Varna, prudently kept his
steamer out of the reach of the Turkish
guns. Marshal Diebitsch undertook the
command on condition that neither the
Czar nor his brother should remain in
Turkey. Since then Nicholas has yielded
to the conviction that he is not able
to conduct a war, and so he has con-
tented himself with commanding at re-
views, and this he does with delight and
fanaticism. He identifies himself with
such manoeuvres so well that he takes
off his helmet once, and cries out, "Boys,
follow US into the fray!" Another time
he gives his aide-de-camp an order to
charge, and, forgetting that there was no
danger, he says, "Fight your way through;
care not for your family, I will provide
for them." Obliged to surrender Peters-
burgh, he puts this clause in the capitu-

lation, that the Winter Palace and the
Imperial family shall be preserved; if
not, he will fight to the last drop of his
blood! He is never victorious but al-
ways beaten.

Last year he was surrounded by Gen-
eral Rudiger, and a division marched TO
cut him off from the last hamlet for his
retreat. An aide-de-camp, and after-
wards the Minister of War himself,
came to the commander of this division,
to persuade him not to perform this ma-
nguvre, but he says, in reply, that he
must obey his immediate chief. Then
they address the same prayer to General
Rudiger. "I should like to save his Ma-
jesty," answered the old warrior, "but,
how is it to be managed! Now, my
weakest point is here; let the Emperor
attack it—let him kill my artillerymen
and break through, I will do nothing to
prevent it, if it happened as he advised."
And the Czar, full of joy, said, "Ares moi
my artillerymen a splendid idea!" In every
company, namely, eleven carabineers
have been appointed, whose rifles reach
to the distance of 1900 paces, in imita-
tion of the Austrian Infantry.

At night he gives orders that the al-
arm shall not be sounded before 8 o'
clock in the morning, yet to send him
reports every hour. He wraps himself
up in his cloak and slumbers. The
General who has to send the reports has
them all in readiness, and goes to bed
ordering paper to be taken every hour
from the table and carried to the Em-
peror.

on horses in searching for the enemy, whom
he could not meet with. He calls the
commander of the detachment, and says
to him, "Why did not see you?—were
you afraid?" "I have neither cavalry nor
artillery; must keep in the forest an-
d swear I am the General." The Czar arreste
him, and the General who succeeded
him, in order to avoid the same fate. He
drove the division before the eyes of His
Majesty. The Czar, suffered himself to be beaten, but
escaped the anger of his Majesty. An
Emperor such as this is to conquer this
world!

ing room, Nicholas opened her album
and stood looking at a drawing, lost
in thought. His wife ventured to inquire
as to the subject of his thoughts. The
subject of the drawing was "Godefroy de

grand enterprise," said the Czar, understanding
the nature of so great a design. "Yes, it
is so to go to war for the sake of an idea, to fight

THURSDAY Senate.—Mr. Fessenden, the new Senator from Maine, appeared and was sworn.

Another batch of petitions against the repeal of the Missouri Compromise was presented.

Mr. Cass presented petition asking the interposition of this Government with foreign powers to secure to American citizens abroad the enjoyment of religious worship and place of sepulture, and spoke in favor of the movement.

The Nebraska bill was taken up, and Mr. Toombs spoke at length in support of the bill.

House. Mr. Disney, from the committee on public lands, reported back the Senate bill granting two millions and half acres of land to Wisconsin for railroads in that State. A debate ensued, and then no quorum being present the House adjourned.

FRIDAY.—Senate. Mr. Everett presented the resolutions of the Legislature of Massachusetts against the repeal of the Missouri Compromise. Mr. Sumner presented the remonstrance of Harriet Beecher Stowe and eleven hundred women of Andover, Massachusetts, and also of eleven hundred men of the same place, against the repeal of the Missouri Compromise. Several similar petitions from Indiana and Ohio were also presented.

Mr. Walker reported bill extending the rights of pre-emption to actual settlers. He said this bill would probably take the place of the Homestead bill, and it came nearer than any other measure to securing homesteads to actual settlers.

The Nebraska bill was taken up. Mr. Douglas said that the friends of the bill supposal that all discussion proposed by its opponents had taken place and had considered when would be the proper time to vote upon it. They had come to the conclusion to continue the debate till Tuesday. On Wednesday he would close the debate and the Senate could vote on the bill. Mr. Chase said as he had previously given notice he had numerous amendments to offer. He would at the proper time be in the way of getting the question. Mr. Hunter then spoke in support of the bill. Without conducting, he gave way for a motion to postpone.

House.—Mr. Stratton presented resolutions of the Legislature of New Jersey, and Mr. Faulkner resolutions of the Legislature of Virginia asking for additional grants of lands to soldiers of the war of 1812. Referred to the Military committee.

Mr. Stanton, of Kentucky, made unanimous report from the committee Elections, concluding with a resolution that Jose Gailegos is entitled to his seat as a delegate from New Mexico, over William Car Lane, the contestant. The former receiving majority of 708 votes. Resolution adopted.

Mr. Taylor, of Ohio, asked leave to offer resolution instructing the Select Committee appointed to enquire into the expediency of amending the constitution relative to the election of President and Vice President, further to inquire into the expediency of limiting the service of the President to one term, and making him thereafter ineligible. Objected to.

A bill was reported from the Committee on Public Lands, in reference to Schools. Mr. Letcher objected strenuously to its passage and it was referred.

Mr. Churchwell announced the death of Robert Armstrong, printer to the House, passing in high virtue, and moved when the House adjourned it be to Monday, to enable members to attend his funeral. Agreed to.

Senate.—Mr. Cass called attention to some remarks of Lord Clarendon in the British Parliament, in reference to the close alliance between England and France, which he thought conveyed the idea that those countries entertained designs against the United States. Messrs. Mason and Weller objected to the general "abstractions," and the matter was dropped.

The Nebraska bill was taken up, and Messrs. Butler, Brown, and Dodge, of Iowa, spoke in favor of it.

SPAIN.—The papers for several weeks past have been talking good deal of coup d'état, which was about to take place, by which the Duke of Alba, brother-in-law to Louis Napoleon, was to be elevated to the throne. We learn from the London Times that coup d'état is meditated but its object is very different from that represented. The scheme is to unite Spain and Portugal, and make Pedro, the young King of Portugal, the ruler of both countries under the title of Emperor. The Times correspondent writes that the shameless profligacy of the Queen has excited an intense and universal disgust among the Spanish masses—and that circulars are scattered throughout the country calling upon the people to rise and throw off the yoke of their infamous Queen and her profligate and imbecile favourite. The Portuguese connexion is openly avowed. The Spanish people are said to be wary of the Bourbons—they are also very jealous of French influence—and the present union between England and France excites great uneasiness among them.

It is supposed that some decided movement looking to the dethronement of the Queen and the elevation of Pedro, cannot be long deferred.

To all persons concerned in the estate of Alpheus Hall, late of Milton, in said district, deceased. GREETINGS:

5. RESOLVED, That in so far as the traffic in ardent spirits affects the social, civil and pecuniary interests of the country, it is a political question, as much as any other within the range of our police and revenue laws, or as that of cleaning out a river for navigation, or constructing a public road and is as clearly entitled TO be so recognized and dealt with. HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, December 18.

Mr. TAYLOR, of Ohio, said I did not intend to participate in this debate and should have simply given a silent vote upon the resolution, the debate called by had not assumed a character of very great interest.

I think the country is indebted to the gentleman from Maryland Mr. SOULÉ for introducing it and my friend from Virginia Mr. DALY will withdraw his motion to refer it to the Committee on Foreign Affairs.

I will not detain the House further than to say that I believe the impression very generally prevailing in the country is strongly antagonistic to the appointment of foreign-born citizens to represent the nation in foreign courts. If it is true that we have had official information that this secret meeting held at Ostend was held, it is well known that such meeting did take place. There is not a gentleman in this House who will deny it. And if it did take place, it must have been for an object. There is that object; the sooner the people of this country know it from the proper source the better.

The gentleman from Alabama Mr. PHILLIPS told the House, as I understood him, that he should vote to send the resolution to the Committee on Foreign Affairs for the purpose of giving it the go-by. Well, SIR, I have the highest respect for that committee, admire their representative character, and the work pursued by them during the last session, alluded to by my friend from Virginia. MR. BAYLY commanded my admiration for its conservativeness. But when a gentleman wishes to have the resolution given the go-by by referring it to one of the standing committees of the House, I cannot vote for such reference, say that it is due to this House, the representatives of the nation. It is due to the dignity of the House, that we should call upon the Chief Executive of the nation for such information as he can give us, incompatible with the public interest, touching this meeting of foreign ministers abroad.

Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Minister of the United States in London, the Minister at Paris, the Minister of the United States at Madrid, and the Minister at the Hague—two of them, Mr. SOULÉ and Mr. BELMONT, men of foreign birth—were invited by themselves or by each other, directed by the Government of the United States to meet at Ostend in Belgium, whether for an important purpose or for no purpose, has certainly attracted a great deal of the attention of the people of this country; and it is not premature to call for information respecting it. We are not acting upon reports. The Chief Executive, who sent a message to this House yesterday, has stated officially that a misunderstanding has recently taken place between France and the United States because the authorities of France had refused permission for Mr. SOULÉ to pass through that country his way from the meeting at Ostend by London to his post in Madrid. It is not, therefore, a mere matter of report upon which we are acting; it is upon something much more tangible.

Now, sir, what is it that produced that misunderstanding with France, for which an ample apology was made, if not this? If we may believe newspaper reports, when Mr. SOULÉ refused permission to pass through France, Mr. MASON demanded an apology, it being considered a direct insult to the country. But the matter was explained by saying that Mr. SOULÉ had not refused the Minister of the United States, but as a private citizen who had formerly resided in France and who had for cause been a fugitive from that country in his early days, and having contracted the dislike of that Government, he was prohibited from passing through the country until the Minister in France interposed, and the prohibition withdrawn.

But sir, this meeting at Ostend has attracted a great deal of interest in this country, and I think every gentleman in the House must admit that it is proper to call upon the President of the United States for the information in his possession, if it be given without prejudice to the public interest.

Sir, the public is nearly unanimous in opposition to sending for ministers abroad, such as Messrs. SOULÉ and BELMONT. Do not speak of it as a matter of much importance, but will mention the fact that about a year ago, in travelling in Holland and the Hague itself, in Amsterdam, in the Netherlands, in the United Provinces, almost as much a Republic as ourselves, although they are a limited monarchy—everywhere heard complaints made in advance of the appointment of a foreign-born citizen to represent the people of America. It was said by them that they had deserved better treatment at the hands of the United States, because in the days of the revolution they had loaned freely their power, their money, and their influence to establish the liberty of this country. They said they deserved least to have a man to represent us who is not an American citizen.

I know nothing personally against Mr. BELMONT, but I repeat, the people of the country almost unanimously, a vast majority of them, disapprove of the appointment of such men to such high places in the diplomacy of the nation. Sir, I say to this House, that neither Mr. SOULÉ nor Mr. BELMONT, whatever be their talents or wealth, are the proper persons to represent the people of America in foreign courts. I say it here in my place. I have the right to say it, as a representative called upon yearly to vote the salaries of these men; that proper men, whose antecedents are unexceptionable, should be appointed to represent abroad. I am prepared to say that no citizen of foreign birth should be appointed. Mr. GALLATIN was sent to England by Mr. ADAMS, but Mr. GALLATIN had filled some of the highest offices of the country and had shown himself eminently capable, honest, and faithful to the Constitution of the United States. But SIR, the object of these gentlemen who have recently been appointed ought to be made known to the people of this country, and there is no more appropriate mode of making it known than by a respectful call upon the President of the United States to communicate this information, if it be incompatible with the public interests. If these gentlemen were not authorized by the Government to go to Ostend, then the Government is not responsible for their action; they deserted their posts to the injury of the Government, and that is another objection to them.

Mr. Speaker, the fashion nowadays of ex-consuls, ex-ministers, and gentlemen in high official positions writing what are called flattering letters to foreign towns, and stirring up bad feeling against the Government of the United States, is anything but kind, generous, or conservative of the peace of the country. Sir, I have a Chief Magistrate who is authorized to send ministers to foreign countries, and so long as the ministers thus appointed do their duty under the instructions of the Executive and uphold the honor, the rights, the dignity, and the interests of the Republic of the United States abroad, they shall have my aid and support. But when they step out of their proper sphere to play the Red Republican assailant and attempt to revolutionize governments abroad, or to form entangling alliances with foreign nations, a citizen, as long as he has the right to do so, should not have said a word upon this occasion if the resolution had been permitted to take the usual course.

MOSES DRISCOLL, Sheriff of the County, reports that this month a party of Indians made descent upon the rancho of Jesus Gaess and twelve head of cattle. Information was received from Francisco Lopez, the Judge of the Probate Court of the County of San Miguel, who directed the Sheriff of the Peace of the First District to collect the facts. More of the stock has been recovered and after the officials have inflicted punishment.

Lou Salazar of San Miguel, and of the party of two buffalo hunters who went out upon the plains near the end of November, was killed by the Indians on the 13th day of December under the following circumstances: The party of hunters he was with separated from those from Taos and Rabbit Hog, followed down the Nutel some distance and then struck the prairie toward the Cimarron, in which region they found sufficiency of buffalo. Having completed their hunt, Pedro Gonzales went to cut grass, taking with him five mules; one hour after, the Indians made an appearance at the camp and drove off nearly all their animals.

They were pursued by Jose Guadalupe Salazar, his brother, and one servant who were attacked and killed by the Indians, but the third hid himself in the grass, and could not be found. One of the Indians, after he was shot, died shortly and was buried on the spot. They looked for Pedro Gonzales and his little party until sundown, and as they could not find traces of them, it is supposed they fell into the hands of the Indians. They were obliged to leave all the proceeds of the hunt behind them. The above facts may be relied upon; they were communicated to the Governor officially by the Justice of the Peace and Judge of the Probate Court of San Miguel County.

ARRIVAL OF MAJOR BLAKE AND CAPT. EWE.
Major Blake, from Fort Sumner, Taos, and Capt. Ewe from Albuquerque, both of the Dragoons, arrived in town on Saturday evening last. The latter returned short time since from his trip to the White Mountains, where he was ordered on an exploring expedition, but failed to obtain any information of importance.

DEATH OF GEN. ARMIJO.
A report has reached us, and at this time is well authenticated, to leave no doubt as to the death of Gen. Armijo. He died at his residence in the Acoma one day last week after long and painful illness. He occupied in time past a conspicuous place in the history of this country, and for many years Governor of New Mexico. When the Territory fell into the hands of the Americans, he retired from public life and lived as a private country gentleman up to the day of his death. Peace to his ashes!
